course.title: React Fundamentals
course.description: Thinking in components: element trees as plain data, pure components and props, composition, lists and keys, minimal state, immutable updates, and controlled-form logic.

lessons.title: Elements and What JSX Compiles To
lessons.explanation:
## The UI is just data React's big idea: your UI is **a value** — a tree of plain objects describing what should be on screen — and components are functions that return that value. JSX is only syntax sugar for building the tree: ```jsx // What you write:

Hello

// What it compiles to (conceptually): h('div', { className: 'row' }, h('h1', {}, 'Hello') ) ``` Each `h` call (React calls it `React.createElement` / the JSX runtime) returns a plain object. In this course we work with that object directly, no React needed: **Element convention (used in every exercise of this course):** an element is a plain object `{ type, props, children }` — `type` is a tag string like `'div'` or `'h1'`, `props` is an object (use `{}` when empty; attributes like `className` or `href` live here), and `children` is an array whose items are elements or strings (use `[]` when empty). So the `
` above is: ```js { type: 'div', props: { className: 'row' }, children: [ { type: 'h1', props: {}, children: ['Hello'] } ] } ``` JSX rules worth knowing before you ever install React: an expression must return **one** root element (hence wrapper divs and fragments); attributes are camelCase JavaScript props — `className` not `class`, `onClick` not `onclick`; and `{ }` switches from markup back into JavaScript, so `

{count + 1}

` embeds a computed child. ### Common mistakes - Thinking JSX is HTML. It is function calls in costume — which is why `class` (a JS keyword) became `className`. - Returning two sibling elements from a component. Two roots = two return values = impossible for one function call. - Quoting expressions: `` passes the literal string `"{url}"`; `src={url}` passes the variable.

lessons.title: Components as Pure Functions of Props
Composition and children
lessons.explanation:
## Components that contain things A layout component doesn't know what goes inside it — the caller decides. JSX nesting delivers the inner content as the `children` prop: ```jsx

42 users

 // compiles to: Card({ title: 'Stats', children: [ h('p', {}, '42 users') ] }) function Card({ title, children }) { return (

{title}

{children}
); } ``` Walking through it: whatever the caller nests between `` and `` arrives as an array of already-built elements in `props.children`. Card never inspects them — it just places them into its own tree (here, spread into the card-body's children). **In this course, `children` is always an array of elements/strings**, and "placing children" means using that array (or spreading it) as some node's children. Because elements are plain values, they can also travel through *any* prop, not just children — a `header` slot, a `footer` slot, an `icon` prop. And since components are plain functions, a component can be passed as a prop too and called by the receiver. This is **composition**: big UIs assembled from small parts that each own one job, instead of one component with thirty options. ### Common mistakes - Rebuilding what you were given. Children arrive *already built* — place them, don't reconstruct them. - Hardcoding content that should be a slot — if two screens need different footers, the footer is a prop. - Forgetting that `{children}` inside a wrapper element nests the whole ARRAY as that element's children.

lessons.title: Conditional Rendering
Rendering Lists and Keys
State: the Minimal Source of Truth
Events and Immutable Updates
lessons.explanation:
## Next state = f(current state, event)

When the user acts, React calls your handler, and the handler's job is to compute the **next state** from the current one. The cardinal rule: **never mutate — replace.**

```js
// WRONG: mutation. The array is still the SAME object...
todos.push({ text, done: false });
// ...so React compares old === new, sees the same reference, and may not re-render.

// RIGHT: a new array containing the old items plus one.
const next = [...todos, { id: nextId, text, done: false }];
```

React detects change by **reference comparison** — cheap and reliable, but only if changed data is *new* data. The update toolkit is small:

```js
[...arr, item]                               // add
arr.filter((t) => t.id !== id)               // remove
arr.map((t) => t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)   // change one
{ ...state, count: state.count + 1 }         // change a field
```

Read the map line carefully: the one matching todo is rebuilt via object spread, every other todo is reused **as-is**. That is the efficiency model — new containers along the changed path, shared references everywhere else.

These exercises grade both the result **and** the discipline: tests verify your inputs were not mutated and that you returned a new object/array.

### Common mistakes

- `push`, `splice`, `sort`, and `arr[i] =` — all in-place. (`sort` needs a copy first.)
- Spreading the array but mutating an object inside it: `[...todos]` copies the LIST, not the todos. Change a todo → spread that todo too.
- Deriving next state from anything other than the current state passed in.

lessons.title: Controlled Forms as Pure Logic
lessons.explanation:
## The form is an object

In a **controlled form**, the single source of truth is a state object; inputs display it and events update it:

```jsx
const [form, setForm] = useState({ email: '', password: '' });

<input
  name="email"
  value={form.email}                                        // display FROM state
  onChange={(e) => setForm(updateField(form, e.target.name, e.target.value))}  // update INTO state
/>
```

The input shows exactly `form.email` — always. Typing fires onChange, which computes the next form object; the re-render pushes the new value back into the input. The loop state → input → event → state is the controlled-input mental model, and everything interesting in it is **pure logic**:

```js
function updateField(form, name, value) {
  return { ...form, [name]: value };        // one handler serves every field
}
const errors = validate(form);              // derived — never stored
const canSubmit = Object.keys(errors).length === 0;
```

Validation is last lesson's derivation discipline applied to forms: errors are **computed from the form on every render**, not stored next to it, so they can never go stale. The remaining refinement is *when to show them* — the `touched` pattern tracks which fields the user has visited so pristine fields aren't shouting "Required" before anyone typed.

This lesson builds the whole kit: field updaters, validators, visibility rules, submit gates, serializers.

### Common mistakes

- Storing errors in state and updating them "when things change" — they drift. Derive them.
- One onChange per field, each hard-coding its own key. The `name` attribute + computed property handles all fields with one function.
- Parsing as the user types ("age must be a number" while they typed `1`…). Keep raw strings in form state; parse on validate/submit.

hints: Count first, then map the count to its display form.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `progressLabel` that takes todos `{ done }` and returns `'<completed> of <total> done'`, e.g. `'2 of 5 done'` (works for empty: `'0 of 0 done'`).
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Both numbers in the label derive from one array, so they can never contradict each other — unlike the apps where the header says 2/5 and the list shows 3 items because someone cached a count.
hints: Count the done ones; the total is just length.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `visibleSorted` that a two-step derivation: takes `(items, query, sortBy)` with items `{ id, name, cents }`; filters by case-insensitive name match, then sorts the result by `sortBy` — `'name'` (ascending, use < comparison) or `'cents'` (ascending). Does not mutate the input.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: State is three small values (items, query, sortBy); the on-screen list is one pipeline over them. Note the trick: filter() already produced a fresh array, so sorting it in place mutates nothing the caller owns.
hints: filter returns a NEW array — sorting that copy is safe. Branch inside the comparator.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
A todo screen stores ONLY this state: `{ todos: [{ id, text, done }], filter: 'all' | 'active' | 'completed' }`.

Export `deriveView(state)` returning everything the UI needs, all derived:

- `visible`: todos the current filter shows (active = not done), in original order
- `remaining`: count of not-done todos (regardless of filter)
- `allDone`: whether every todo is done (true when the list is empty)
- `summary`: the string `'<remaining> left'`, e.g. `'2 left'`
- `emptyMessage`: `null` when `visible` is non-empty; otherwise `'Nothing here'` for filters `'active'`/`'completed'` or `'Add your first todo'` for `'all'`
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Two stored values fan out into five rendered facts, every one recomputed per call, so no combination of toggles and filter switches can ever show contradictory UI. This function is what the body of a real todo component looks like above its return statement — and because it is pure, it tests like this, without rendering anything.
hints: Each output field is one small derivation — write them one at a time.
remaining counts across ALL todos, not just the visible ones.
emptyMessage depends on both the visible result and which filter produced it.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Why does `todos.push(newTodo)` break React updates while `[...todos, newTodo]` works?
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Deep-comparing every render would be ruinously slow, so React asks one cheap question: same reference? A mutated array answers "same" and the UI silently skips updating — the most classic React bug. New state must be a new object.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: To toggle `todos[2].done`, is `const next = [...todos]; next[2].done = !next[2].done;` safe?
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Spread is shallow: the new array holds the SAME object references. Mutating next[2] mutates the one shared todo. The correct shape rebuilds the changed element: `todos.map((t, i) => i === 2 ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)` — new array AND a new object on the changed path.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: In this course, a handler like `addTodo(todos, text)` models what part of real React?
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: In real code: `onClick={() => setTodos(addTodo(todos, text))}`. The wiring (onClick, setTodos) is React plumbing; the interesting, bug-prone part is the pure function computing next state — which is why it is what these exercises grade, and why real teams extract and unit-test exactly these.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: The "change one item" idiom is `arr.map((t) => t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)`. What do the unchanged items get?
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Immutability does not mean copying everything — it means new objects along the changed path only. Reusing untouched references is what keeps this fast and lets React (and memoized children) skip re-rendering rows whose reference did not change.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `addTodo` that takes `(todos, text)` and returns a NEW array with a todo appended: `{ id, text, done: false }` where id is one more than the highest existing id (1 for an empty list).

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The add idiom: one spread, one fresh object. The id derivation comes from last lesson — handlers routinely combine a derivation with a replacement.
hints: Derive the id (max + 1), then spread-append.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `toggleTodo` that takes `(todos, id)` and returns a new array where the matching todo has `done` flipped — rebuilt with object spread — and every other todo is untouched.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: THE signature immutable update: map rebuilds the array, the ternary rebuilds only the matching element, `...t` preserves its other fields. Memorize this line — you will type it hundreds of times.
hints: map; ternary on the id; spread the matching todo with done flipped.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `removeTodo` that takes `(todos, id)` and returns a new array without the matching todo.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Removal is filtering — no splice, no index hunting. An unknown id harmlessly returns an equal (but new) array; delete-twice bugs simply cannot corrupt anything.
hints: filter keeps everything whose id does NOT match.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `renameTodo` that takes `(todos, id, text)` and returns a new array with the matching todo's text replaced (other fields intact).

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The map-ternary-spread template parameterizes cleanly: swap which field the spread overrides and you have rename, toggle, assign, star, archive… one pattern, every single-item edit.
hints: Same shape as toggle, different field.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `clearCompleted` that takes todos and returns a new array containing only the not-done ones.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Bulk removal is the same filter as single removal with a different predicate. The surviving todos are reused by reference — only the list itself is new.
hints: One filter.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `toggleAll` that takes todos and returns a new array where ALL todos are marked done — unless every one is already done, in which case all become not-done (the standard toggle-all checkbox behavior).

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Derive-then-update: the target state is computed ONCE from the whole list, then applied uniformly. Flipping each todo individually would be a different (and wrong) feature — mixed lists would stay mixed.
hints: Derive the target boolean first (every), then map everything to it.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `increment` that takes a state object `{ count, step }` and returns a NEW state with count increased by step (other fields preserved).

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Object updates mirror array updates: spread the old, override the changed key. The next value is computed FROM the state argument — the pure-function discipline that makes updates predictable under rapid events.
hints: Spread the state, override count.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `setStateField` that a generic field setter: takes `(state, key, value)` and returns a new object with that one key replaced: `setStateField({ a: 1, b: 2 }, 'b', 9)` → `{ a: 1, b: 9 }`. Use a computed property name.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The computed-property spread is the engine under every generic form handler and setState wrapper: one function updates any field immutably. You will meet it again in the forms lesson as updateField.
hints: { ...state, [key]: value } — square brackets make the key dynamic.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `selectItem` that takes `(state, id)` where state is `{ items, selectedId }` and returns a new state with selectedId set to id — clicking the already-selected item deselects it (selectedId becomes null).

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Toggle-on-reclick in one expression — the next selection derives from the current one. Note what is NOT here: no copying of the items or the selected object; the id is the whole selection state (last lesson's design, this lesson's update).
hints: A ternary comparing the current selection to the clicked id.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `addToCart` that takes `(cart, product)` where cart items are `{ id, name, cents, qty }` and product is `{ id, name, cents }`. If the product is already in the cart, return a new cart with its qty increased by 1; otherwise append it with qty 1.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Upsert, immutably: a lookup chooses between the change-one idiom and the append idiom. Note `{ ...product, qty: 1 }` also copies the product — the cart must own its rows, not alias the catalog's objects.
hints: find decides the branch: map-with-increment, or spread-append with qty 1.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `changeQty` that takes `(cart, id, qty)` and returns a new cart with that item's qty set — but when qty is 0 or less, the item is removed entirely.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: One user intent ("set the quantity") maps to two structural updates depending on the value — business rules live in the handler, and both branches stay immutable. Stepper-to-zero removing the row is standard cart UX.
hints: Branch first on qty <= 0: filter in that case, map otherwise.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `moveUp` that takes `(items, id)` with items `{ id, name }` and returns a new array where the matching item swapped places with the one before it. If it is already first (or not found), return a **new copy** in the same order.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Immutability is about ownership, not purity theater: once `[...items]` creates an array you own, index assignment inside it is legal — the caller's array is untouched. Copy at the boundary, then work freely.
hints: Copy first, then swapping inside YOUR copy is fine.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `markAllRead` that takes messages `{ id, read }` and returns a new array with every message's read set to true (each message a new object).

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Bulk edits map every element through the spread-override — compare toggleAll. Each message object is rebuilt because each one changed; the unread badge (a derivation!) falls to zero on its own.
hints: map everything through { ...m, read: true }.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `appendLog` that takes `(entries, entry, max)` — appends the entry string and keeps only the LAST max entries: `appendLog(["a", "b"], "c", 2)` → `["b", "c"]`.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Append-with-eviction in one chain: the spread builds the new list, the negative slice trims history. Activity feeds, undo stacks and chat windows all cap state growth exactly like this.
hints: Append, then slice(-max) keeps the tail.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `toggleFlag` that takes `(state, key)` and returns a new object with that boolean field flipped: `toggleFlag({ open: false, pinned: true }, 'open')` → `{ open: true, pinned: true }`.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: setStateField's sibling for booleans — the next value is read from the CURRENT state and negated, in the same expression that replaces it. Sidebars, modals, mute buttons: one generic flipper.
hints: Computed property + negation of the current value.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `mergeSettings` that takes `(settings, patch)` and returns a new object with the patch's keys overriding the current settings: `mergeSettings({ theme: 'light', lang: 'en' }, { theme: 'dark' })` → `{ theme: 'dark', lang: 'en' }`.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The double spread is the immutable PATCH: unchanged keys flow from the old object, the patch overrides what it names, and spread order decides the winner. This is also exactly how setState-with-objects merged in classic React.
hints: Two spreads in order — later keys win.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `dismiss` that takes `(notifications, id)` with items `{ id, text }` and returns a new array without the dismissed one — plus the generic lesson: works for ANY id-keyed list.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Identical to removeTodo with string keys — the idioms are type-agnostic. Toast stacks, alert bars, undo chips: one filter. When you find yourself writing it a third time, extract the generic removeById(list, id).
hints: The removal filter, with string ids this time.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export a handler `setWithHistory` that takes `(state, value)` where state is `{ value, history }` and returns a new state: the old value pushed onto a NEW history array, and the new value installed. `setWithHistory({ value: 1, history: [] }, 5)` → `{ value: 5, history: [1] }`.

**Immutability is graded:** the tests deep-snapshot your arguments before the call, verify them unchanged after, and require the returned value to be a new object/array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Undo support falls out of immutability almost for free: because nothing is ever overwritten in place, remembering the past is just keeping references. The nested history array gets its own spread — new containers along every changed path.
hints: The new history is [...old history, old value].

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Unify the handlers into one **reducer** — the (state, action) => nextState shape of useReducer and Redux. Export `todosReducer(todos, action)` handling:

- `{ type: 'add', text }` → append `{ id: max+1 (1 if empty), text, done: false }`
- `{ type: 'toggle', id }` → flip that todo's done
- `{ type: 'remove', id }` → drop that todo
- `{ type: 'clearCompleted' }` → keep only not-done todos
- any other type → return a shallow **copy** of the todos array unchanged

Never mutate the input.

**Immutability is graded:** inputs are snapshotted and compared after the call; the return value must be a new array.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: A reducer centralizes every legal state transition behind named actions: the component dispatches intent ({ type: "toggle", id }), the reducer owns the how. Each branch is one of this lesson's idioms, which is the real insight — "reducers" are nothing but your immutable handlers gathered into one testable function. This exact signature is what React's useReducer wants.
hints: Each case is one of the handlers you already wrote — a reducer is just their switchboard.
The default case still must not return the input array itself here — return a copy.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: What makes an input "controlled"?
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Controlled means the component owns the value: what the input shows IS form state, keystroke by keystroke. The payoff: validation, formatting, clearing, and prefilling are all plain state operations — no reaching into the DOM to ask an input what it currently holds.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: How does ONE onChange handler serve ten different form fields?
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The event tells you which field fired (target.name) and what it now holds (target.value); a computed-property spread does the rest. Adding an eleventh field means adding an input with a name — zero new handler code. This is the updateField you are about to write.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Where should validation errors live?
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Errors are a pure function of the form: validate(form) recomputed each render is always exactly current. Stored errors are the drift bug again — fix the email, submit, and the stale "invalid email" blocks you. touched is genuine state (it records user behavior); errors never are.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: A fresh signup form shows "Required" under every empty field before the user types anything. The standard fix?
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Two separate derivations: whether a field IS invalid (from form) and whether to SAY so (from touched). Submit-only validation loses live feedback; the touched gate keeps feedback immediate but polite. visibleErrors(errors, touched) below implements exactly this.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export `updateField` — the universal field updater: takes `(form, name, value)` and returns a new form object with that key set: `updateField({ email: '', pw: '' }, 'email', 'a@b.c')` → `{ email: 'a@b.c', pw: '' }`.

**Immutability is graded:** inputs are snapshotted and must be unchanged; the return value must be a new object.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The heart of every controlled form: one immutable setter for all fields, driven by the input's name. Every keystroke in every field of every form you will build flows through this exact line.
hints: Spread plus computed property — one line.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export `toggleCheckbox` — takes `(form, name)` and returns a new form with that boolean field flipped (checkboxes report clicks, not values).

**Immutability is graded:** inputs are snapshotted and must be unchanged; the return value must be a new object.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Checkboxes are the one control where the next value comes from current state rather than the event (e.target.checked works too — this version needs only the name). Same spread, different value source.
hints: Like updateField, but the new value is !form[name].

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export `touchField` — takes `(touched, name)` — the touched-tracking object — and returns a new object with that field marked true: `touchField({}, 'email')` → `{ email: true }`. Called from onBlur.

**Immutability is graded:** inputs are snapshotted and must be unchanged; the return value must be a new object.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: touched is real state — it records something underivable (where the user has been). It only ever grows toward true: once you have visited a field, it stays touched for the life of the form.
hints: Spread, set [name]: true.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export `resetForm` — takes `(form, initial)` and returns a fresh **copy** of initial (not the initial object itself — state objects should not be shared).

**Immutability is graded:** inputs are snapshotted and must be unchanged; the return value must be a new object.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The Cancel button. Copying initial matters: if the same initial object became live state, a later (buggy) mutation of state would corrupt the template every future reset uses. Defensive copies at ownership boundaries.
hints: Return { ...initial } — a copy, not the reference.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export `updateAddress` — takes `(form, key, value)` where form is `{ name, address: { city, zip } }`, and sets a key INSIDE address immutably: both the form object AND the address object must be new: `updateAddress({ name: 'A', address: { city: '', zip: '' } }, 'city', 'Berlin')` → address `{ city: 'Berlin', zip: '' }`.

**Immutability is graded:** inputs are snapshotted and must be unchanged; the return value must be a new object.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Nested state needs a new object at EVERY level along the changed path — the shallow-spread trap from the events lesson, solved by spreading each layer. Deeply nested forms are why many teams keep form state flat.
hints: Two spreads: the outer form and the inner address.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `requiredError` that takes a string value and returns `'Required'` when it is empty **after trimming**, else `''`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The most basic validator, with the detail that separates good forms from annoying ones: "   " is not a name. Validators here return message-or-empty-string so they compose into errors objects cleanly.
hints: trim first — whitespace-only is still empty.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `emailError` that takes an email string and returns `''` when it looks plausible (contains exactly one `@` with at least one character before it and a `.` somewhere after it), else `'Invalid email'`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: A pragmatic plausibility check — real email validation is "send a confirmation link"; the client just catches obvious typos. indexOf twice detects duplicates without a regex, and slicing after the @ scopes the dot requirement to the domain.
hints: indexOf/lastIndexOf for the single-@ rule; check the domain part for a dot.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `minLengthError` that takes `(value, min)` and returns `''` when the value has at least min characters, else `'Must be at least <min> characters'`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Parameterized validators cover whole families of rules; the message interpolates its own threshold so the UI never hardcodes "8" separately from the check (another two-truths drift avoided).
hints: Compare length, build the message with the min baked in.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `confirmError` that takes `(password, confirm)` and returns `''` when they match, else `'Passwords do not match'`. An empty confirm returns the error too (it certainly doesn't match).
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: A cross-field validator: it reads TWO form fields, which is why validate(form) takes the whole form rather than running field validators in isolation. Field rules compose; cross-field rules need the full picture.
hints: Strict string equality.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `passwordChecks` that takes a password and returns the checklist object `{ minLength, hasNumber, hasUpper }` — booleans for: at least 8 chars, contains a digit, contains an uppercase letter. (This powers those live requirement checklists.)
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The live checklist UI (as you type, requirements tick green) is this derivation re-run per keystroke — controlled inputs make it trivial because state always holds the current text. Each ✓/✗ row renders one boolean.
hints: Three independent booleans; character-class regexes for the two scans.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `passwordError` that takes a password and returns `''` when ALL of the three checks pass (≥8 chars, a digit, an uppercase letter), else `'Password too weak'`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The same three rules as passwordChecks, collapsed into a gate — checklist for live feedback, single verdict for the errors object. Two views over one rule set; keep the rules in sync (or build one from the other).
hints: AND the three conditions; one message.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `validateLogin` that takes a login form `{ email, password }` and returns an errors object containing ONLY the failing fields: email required ('Required' for empty-after-trim) else must contain '@' ('Invalid email'); password required ('Required'). Valid form → `{}`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The errors-object convention: keys mirror form fields, absence means valid, and {} means submittable. The else-if encodes rule priority — "Required" and "Invalid email" should never stack on one field.
hints: Build an empty object, add keys only for failures; required beats format.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `hasErrors` that takes an errors object and returns whether it contains any keys.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The bridge from the errors object to a boolean the UI can branch on. Because errors are derived fresh each render, this verdict is always exactly current.
hints: Object.keys(...).length.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `canSubmit` that takes `(errors, submitting)` and returns whether the submit button is enabled: no error keys AND not already submitting.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The submit gate combines a derivation (validity) with genuine state (an in-flight request). Disabling during submit is the no-double-order guard — the same idempotency instinct as the SQL course's guarded UPDATE.
hints: Two conditions ANDed.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `visibleErrors` that takes `(errors, touched)` and returns only the error entries whose field is touched: `visibleErrors({ email: "Required", pw: "Required" }, { email: true })` → `{ email: "Required" }`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The polite-forms pattern as a pure function: validity (errors) and visibility (touched) stay separate concerns, intersected at the last moment. Submit buttons check errors; error MESSAGES render from visibleErrors.
hints: Copy over only the error keys that are true in touched.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `touchAll` that takes a form object and returns a touched object with every form key set to true — used when the user hits Submit, so all errors become visible at once: `touchAll({ email: '', pw: '' })` → `{ email: true, pw: true }`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The submit-click companion to per-field blur: pressing Submit means the user has implicitly "visited" everything, so visibility gates open everywhere and every problem shows at once instead of one blur at a time.
hints: Map the form keys to true in a fresh object.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `serializeForm` that takes a form object of string values and returns a new object with every value trimmed — what you actually send to the API: `serializeForm({ name: "  Ada ", city: "x" })` → `{ name: "Ada", city: "x" }`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Form state holds what the user typed (spaces and all — editing feels wrong otherwise); the payload holds what the system means. Serialization is the one sanctioned place where those diverge.
hints: Loop the keys, trim each value into a new object.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `parseQuantityField` that takes the raw string from a quantity input and returns the integer when the TRIMMED string is all digits and at least 1 (`'3'` → 3), else `null` — for `''`, `'abc'`, `'1.5'`, `'0'`, and `'-2'` alike.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: Form state kept the raw string while typing; this is the parse-at-the-boundary step. The all-digits regex rejects what Number() would sloppily accept ('1.5' → 1.5, '' → 0), and null — not NaN, not 0 — is the unambiguous "not valid" signal.
hints: Validate the string shape with a regex first, then convert and range-check.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `charsLeft` that takes `(text, max)` and returns the counter object `{ left, over }`: characters remaining (may go negative) and whether the limit is exceeded. `charsLeft('hello', 10)` → `{ left: 5, over: false }`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The tweet-box counter: pure derivation from the controlled text, including the deliberate negative numbers that let the UI show "-2" in red rather than silently truncating what the user typed.
hints: Subtract; over is just left < 0.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions: Export a function `fieldProps` that the wiring helper: takes `(form, name)` and returns the props object a controlled input needs: `{ name, value: form[name] }`. `fieldProps({ email: 'x' }, 'email')` → `{ name: 'email', value: 'x' }`.
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: In JSX this becomes `<input {...fieldProps(form, 'email')} onChange={handle} />` — spread-able prop bundles that keep ten inputs consistent. Tiny helpers like this are how form libraries (Formik's getFieldProps, react-hook-form's register) actually work.
hints: Pull the value out by key; echo the name.

bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.instructions:
Export `signupState(form, touched, submitting)` — the complete derived state for a signup form `{ email, password, confirm }`:

Validation rules (errors object contains only failing fields, first matching rule wins per field):
- email: `'Required'` when empty after trim, else `'Invalid email'` when it doesn't contain `'@'`
- password: `'Required'` when empty, else `'Password too weak'` unless it has ≥8 chars AND a digit AND an uppercase letter
- confirm: `'Passwords do not match'` when it differs from password (an empty confirm with an empty password matches, so no error)

Return `{ errors, visibleErrors, canSubmit }`:
- `errors`: the full validation result
- `visibleErrors`: only the error entries whose field is true in `touched`
- `canSubmit`: no errors at all AND not `submitting`
bootforge/react-fundamentals/lists-and-s.explanation: The entire form brain as one pure, exhaustively-testable function: rules with per-field priority, a cross-field match check, the touched visibility gate, and the submit gate with the in-flight guard. A component using it stores only form, touched, and submitting — three honest pieces of state — and derives every pixel of feedback from this call. That is the controlled-form mental model, complete.
hints: Build the three pieces in order — errors first; the other two derive from it.
Per field: required check first, else-if the format/strength check.
The confirm rule compares the two fields directly; empty-vs-empty is a match, hence no error.
